qa.question_canonical: Why did Franklin run away to Philadelphia?
qa.answer: Franklin fled a bitter, sometimes physically abusive falling-out with his brother and master, James, arriving in Philadelphia broke and unknown -- his famous walk down Market Street eating a bread roll marks the moment his old life ended.

citations.quote: He gave me accordingly three great Puffy Rolls . . . walk'd off with a Roll under each Arm, and eating the other.
citations.full_passage_text: I ask'd for Bisket, meaning such as we had in Boston; that Sort, it seems, was not made in Philadelphia. I then ask'd for a threepenny Loaf, and was told they had none such. So not considering or knowing the Difference of Money, I bade him give me three penny worth of any sort. He gave me accordingly three great Puffy Rolls. I was surpriz'd at the Quantity, but took it, and, having no room in my Pockets, walk'd off with a Roll under each Arm, and eating the other.

qa.answer: The Junto was a club Franklin formed with his most capable friends for mutual improvement -- each meeting required a member to raise a question of morals, politics, or natural philosophy for the group to debate.

citations.quote: I had form'd most of my ingenious Acquaintance into a Club for mutual Improvement, which we called the Junto.
citations.full_passage_text: I should have mention'd before, that, in the Autumn of the preceding Year, I had form'd most of my ingenious Acquaintance into a Club for mutual Improvement, which we called the Junto; we met on Friday Evenings. The Rules I drew up requir'd that every Member, in his Turn, should produce one or more Queries on any Point of Morals, Politics, or Natural Philosophy, to be discuss'd by the Company.

qa.answer: Franklin's project for 'moral perfection' was a list of thirteen named virtues -- including temperance, order, frugality, and industry -- which he tracked one at a time, week by week, in a small book, checking off any day he slipped.

citations.quote: It was about this time I conceiv'd the bold and arduous Project of arriving at moral Perfection.
citations.full_passage_text: It was about this time I conceiv'd the bold and arduous Project of arriving at moral Perfection. I wish'd to live without committing any Fault at any time; I would conquer all that either Natural Inclination, Custom, or Company might lead me into. As I knew, or thought I knew, what was right and wrong, I did not see why I might not always do the one and avoid the other.

qa.answer: Yes -- his electrical experiments spread through the scientific world, earning him election to the Royal Society and its Copley Medal without his ever having applied for the honor.

citations.quote: These Discoveries . . . gain'd me the Honour of being chosen a Member of the Royal Society.
citations.full_passage_text: The Publication of these Discoveries occasion'd me a good deal of Correspondence with several Learned Persons in Europe, and gain'd me the Honour of being chosen a Member of the Royal Society, and, without my having made any Application for it, a handsome Gold Medal was voted to me by that Society.

qa.question_canonical: What civic institutions did Franklin start?
qa.answer: Franklin founded the Library Company of Philadelphia -- which he calls the mother of all North American subscription libraries -- plus the Union Fire Company, a paving and street-lighting initiative, an academy that became the University of Pennsylvania, and the Pennsylvania Hospital.

citations.quote: The Library . . . was the Mother of all the North American Subscription Libraries.
citations.full_passage_text: This Library afforded me the Means of Improvement by constant Study, for which I set apart an Hour or two each Day. The Library, though small, was the Mother of all the North American Subscription Libraries, now so numerous. It is a Common Benefit, and every Room in Philadelphia has since felt its Effects.

qa.question_canonical: What does Poor Richard's Almanack say about waking up early?
qa.answer: Poor Richard's most famous proverb -- 'Early to Bed, and early to rise, makes a Man healthy, wealthy, and wise' -- captures the whole almanack's theme of industry and frugality as the road to prosperity.

citations.quote: Early to Bed, and early to rise, makes a Man healthy, wealthy, and wise.
citations.full_passage_text: In 1732 I first publish'd my Almanack, under the Name of Richard Saunders; it was continu'd by me about 25 years, and came to be in such Demand that I reap'd considerable Profit from it. I fill'd all the little Spaces that occur'd between the Remarkable Days in the Calendar with Proverbial Sentences, chiefly such as inculcated Industry and Frugality, as the Means of procuring Wealth: 'Early to Bed, and early to rise, makes a Man healthy, wealthy, and wise.'
